description:
Founded in 1921, the National Gallery of Armenia brings Armenian art into conversation with art from other countries. Its main museum stands in central Yerevan.

Paintings, sculpture, graphic art and decorative objects form its collections. A network of regional branches also preserves the work of individual Armenian artists and local artistic communities.

The Aichi Prefectural Museum of Art in Nagoya focuses on modern and contemporary art from Japan and abroad. Its collecting policy also gives particular attention to artists connected with Aichi.

European painting, postwar American art and modern Japanese work sit alongside substantial donations from Fujii Tatsukichi and collector Kimura Teizo. These different strands connect regional artistic life with international developments.

Abbey House Museum explores the social history of Leeds through everyday objects and recreated Victorian streets. The museum is in Kirkstall, Leeds.

Its childhood galleries bring together toys and other objects associated with growing up. Shops, household settings and familiar possessions offer a close view of how daily life has changed.

Abbot Hall is an art gallery in a Georgian house beside the River Kent in Kendal. Its collection connects the art of Cumbria with wider developments in British painting and sculpture.

George Romney's portraits and watercolours by Turner and Ruskin are important strands. Modern British holdings include work by Barbara Hepworth, Lucian Freud, Paula Rego and Bridget Riley.

The Museo Nacional del Prado in Madrid opened in 1819. Its collections grew from Spain's royal collections and later additions, creating a setting for studying Spanish painting alongside other European traditions.

The museum also holds sculpture, drawings, prints and decorative objects. These collections extend the story beyond the large paintings for which the Prado is best known.

Munich's municipal art gallery occupies the former villa of painter Franz von Lenbach. Its collection connects nineteenth-century art associated with Munich with modern and contemporary work.

The Blue Rider group is a central focus. Paintings connected with this circle provide a way into the changes in colour, form and subject that shaped early twentieth-century art.

Founded in 1861, the National Gallery of Victoria brings together art and design from different periods and cultures. Its two main Melbourne venues give Australian and international art distinct settings.

NGV International houses the international collections. The Ian Potter Centre: NGV Australia focuses on Indigenous and non-Indigenous Australian art, from historical work to contemporary practice.

The Art Gallery of New South Wales is based in Sydney and collects Australian and international art. Its collections support the study of art across different cultures and periods.

Australian art, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander art, Asian art and international work are important collecting strands. Together they give the gallery both a regional focus and a wider international context.

National Gallery Prague cares for Czech and international art across several buildings. Its palaces, convent and modern exhibition spaces offer different settings for the collections.

The Trade Fair Palace and the palaces around Hradčanské Square are among its Prague venues. The institution also has sites outside the city, so its collection should not be understood as a single building.

The Musée national Picasso-Paris is devoted to Picasso's work and artistic world. It occupies the Hôtel Salé, a seventeenth-century mansion in the Marais district of Paris.

The collection was shaped by transfers from Picasso's heirs to the French state in 1979 and 1990. Its history links the artist's own holdings with the creation of a public museum.

The Hungarian National Gallery traces the development of art in Hungary. Established in Budapest in 1957, it is now associated with the Buda Castle complex.

Its collections include older Hungarian art, nineteenth- and twentieth-century painting, sculpture, prints and drawings. International art after 1800 adds a wider context to the national collections.

The Museum of Fine Arts stands beside Heroes' Square in Budapest. Its collections connect European painting and sculpture with the art of ancient Egypt and the classical world.

Old Master paintings span European schools from the thirteenth century to 1800. Prints, drawings and older Hungarian works broaden the collection beyond the main painting galleries.

The Uffizi occupies Giorgio Vasari's sixteenth-century building in Florence. The former offices of the Medici administration became a setting for collections closely connected with the family's patronage.

Italian painting from the Middle Ages through the Renaissance is a central focus, alongside other European schools. Ancient sculpture, drawings and prints add further perspectives on the history of art.

The State Hermitage Museum in Saint Petersburg grew from the art collecting of Catherine II. Its collections developed across a group of palace and museum buildings.

European painting is one part of a broader museum of art and culture. The history of the Hermitage connects imperial collecting with the later creation and expansion of a public museum.

The State Tretyakov Gallery in Moscow grew from Pavel Tretyakov's collecting, which began in 1856. Its collections follow Russian art across several historical periods and buildings.

Icons and nineteenth-century painting are important parts of the historic collection. Modern and contemporary art extend that account into the twentieth century and beyond.

The Slovak National Gallery has its principal complex on the Danube embankment in Bratislava. It also operates a network of venues in other parts of Slovakia.

Its collections bring historical art into conversation with modern and contemporary work. The gallery also maintains Web umenia, an online resource for exploring digitised artworks from Slovak and Czech institutions.

The Museu Nacional d'Art de Catalunya occupies the Palau Nacional in Barcelona. Its collections trace Catalan art through medieval, Renaissance, Baroque and modern periods.

Romanesque mural and panel painting are particular strengths. Later collections place Catalan Modernism and other artistic developments alongside the museum's medieval heritage.

Founded in 1683, the Ashmolean is the University of Oxford's museum of art and archaeology. Its collections bring objects from different cultures and historical periods into a shared setting for study.

European paintings and drawings sit alongside Asian art, antiquities and coins. Raphael drawings, early Pre-Raphaelite work and modern Chinese paintings are among its notable artistic holdings.

The Fitzwilliam Museum grew from the collection left to the University of Cambridge by Richard Fitzwilliam in 1816. Its permanent building on Trumpington Street opened in 1848.

Paintings, prints, drawings, manuscripts and decorative arts form part of a wider collection that also includes antiquities and coins. Gifts and bequests have continued to shape the museum since its foundation.

Manchester Art Gallery is part of the city's public museum service. Its fine art collections are particularly associated with nineteenth-century British artists and the Pre-Raphaelites.

Earlier European painting and modern British work give the collection a wider historical range. Craft, design and clothing also form part of the collections cared for by Manchester City Galleries.

The Clark Art Institute in Williamstown, Massachusetts, combines an art museum with an institution for research. Its collections include European and American painting, sculpture and works on paper.

Nineteenth-century French painting is a particular focus, including Impressionist work. These holdings sit alongside earlier European art and American painting.

Isabella Stewart Gardner created her Boston museum as a carefully arranged setting for art. It opened to the public in 1903, in a building inspired by the architecture of Venice.

Paintings and architectural fragments reflect Gardner's collecting interests and travels. Her arrangements remain central to understanding the museum, where individual works form part of a larger personal composition.

The Museum of Modern Art in New York was established in 1929. Its collection follows the changing forms of modern and contemporary art through work from around the world.

Painting and sculpture are part of a wider collection that includes drawing, prints, photography, architecture, design, film and performance. This range makes it possible to compare artistic ideas across different media.

The National Gallery of Art in Washington, DC, grew from Andrew Mellon's gift of a collection and a museum building. Its campus on the National Mall includes two main buildings and a sculpture garden.

The West Building is associated with older European and American art. The East Building extends the museum's scope through modern and contemporary work.

The Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum in New York developed from a collection focused on abstract and non-objective art. Its identity connects the study of modern art with Frank Lloyd Wright's distinctive museum building.

The New York collection forms part of the Guggenheim's wider network of collections. Its online catalogue distinguishes work associated with New York, Venice and Bilbao.

The Metropolitan Museum of Art's main building stands on Fifth Avenue in New York. The museum has occupied this site since 1880, expanding its buildings and collections over time.

European painting, American art and classical antiquities are among its collecting areas. Asian art, Islamic art, medieval art, drawings and prints add to the museum's account of art across cultures.

The Smithsonian American Art Museum explores American visual culture from the colonial period to the present. Its main museum is in central Washington, DC.

Painting, sculpture, photography, craft and newer media contribute to this account. The collections include American Impressionism, New Deal art and work by self-taught, African American and Latino artists.

The Louvre occupies a former royal palace in central Paris and opened as a public museum in 1793. Its buildings retain traces of the site's earlier life as a fortress and a royal residence.

The collections range from ancient civilisations to nineteenth-century art. Painting belongs to this broader setting alongside antiquities, sculpture, decorative objects and works on paper.
